item.title: She Let Her Son Rot on the Bathroom Floor❤️
item.description:
When relatives couldn't reach Shannon Lloyd, they requested a welfare check. Officers arrived expecting to check on his wellbeing, but instead uncovered a case that would leave the community stunned. Investigators alleged Shannon, who relied on his mother Cheryl Christensen for care after a childhood brain injury, had suffered a serious fall days earlier and never received medical treatment.
Before Cheryl Christensen could stand trial, the story took another shocking turn. She was found dead in her home in a homicide, and her other son later died following an armed standoff with police, leaving two tragedies intertwined in one extraordinary family case.
Do you think welfare checks are one of the most important tools for uncovering hidden cases, or are they too often requested only after it's already too late?

item.title: A 19-Day-Old Baby At The Center Of A Shocking Case
item.description:
When baby Thea June Wilson was only 19 days old, she was rushed to hospital after becoming seriously unwell. Her mother, Nicole Blain, told investigators her version of events, but as detectives began piecing together the timeline, questions started to emerge.
Police found inconsistencies between the explanation they were given and the evidence they uncovered. During the trial, prosecutors argued that what happened to Thea could not have occurred the way Blain claimed, and after hearing the evidence, a jury found her guilty of murder.
The case of baby Thea left a community searching for answers and facing the heartbreaking question of how the truth was uncovered after such a devastating loss.
What do you think is the most important part of an investigation like this: the evidence, the timeline, or the questions that arise when a story doesn't add up?
